passages.title: God's glory appears among the exiles
passages.summary: Ezekiel is a priest living among the exiles by a river in Babylon. The heavens open, and he sees visions of God. A storm comes from the north with flashing fire. In it are four living creatures, each with four faces and four wings. Beside each is a wheel within a wheel, full of eyes. Above them is a shining platform and a throne like sapphire. On the throne is a figure like a man, surrounded by fire and a rainbow. Ezekiel falls on his face and hears a voice.
passages.uncertainty: This chapter has no mapped places. Visionary settings and uncertain river locations remain unmapped.

lds.text: The 2026 lesson emphasizes God’s presence among exiles. Why does the glory appear among people far from Jerusalem?

contextNote.title: God's glory appears among the exiles
contextNote.text: The vision comes in Babylon, far from the temple. The throne has wheels that move in any direction (verse 17). So God’s presence is not fixed to one place. Verse 28 describes what Ezekiel saw with great caution. It was “the appearance of the likeness” of the LORD’s glory. He does not claim to describe God directly. The rainbow in the storm recalls the sign of mercy in Genesis 9:13.

passages.title: Speaking does not depend on a willing audience
passages.summary: A voice tells Ezekiel to stand on his feet. The Spirit enters him and sets him upright. God sends him to the people of Israel, a rebellious nation. He must say, “This is what the Lord GOD says.” Whether they listen or not, they will know a prophet was among them. He must not fear them, though they are like thorns and scorpions. He must not be rebellious as they are. A hand holds out a scroll full of mourning and woe.
passages.uncertainty: This chapter has no mapped places. Visionary settings and uncertain river locations remain unmapped.

lds.text: The lesson’s opening invites people to hear God’s word. Why must Ezekiel speak even when his listeners refuse?

contextNote.title: Speaking does not depend on a willing audience
contextNote.text: God calls Ezekiel “son of man,” which means a human being. The title follows directly on the vision of glory. Verse 2 says the Spirit had to set him on his feet. Verse 7 defines his task. He must speak whether the people hear or refuse. His success is not measured by their response. Verse 5 names the one sure result: they will know a prophet was there.

passages.title: The messenger must hear before he warns
passages.summary: Ezekiel eats the scroll, and it is as sweet as honey. God says foreigners would listen, but Israel will not. God makes his forehead as hard as flint. The Spirit carries him to the exiles, and he sits stunned for seven days. Then God makes him a watchman for Israel. If he fails to warn the wicked, he will answer for their blood. If he warns them, he has saved his own life. God then makes him unable to speak except when given a message.
passages.uncertainty: This chapter has no mapped places. Visionary settings and uncertain river locations remain unmapped.

lds.text: The lesson connects the watchman’s duty with caring leadership. What makes silence dangerous for the appointed watchman?

contextNote.title: The messenger must hear before he warns
contextNote.text: A watchman stood on the wall and warned of danger. Verse 17 puts hearing before warning. Ezekiel must first receive the word from God’s mouth. Verses 18–21 hold him responsible for giving the warning. They do not hold him responsible for the result. A watchman who keeps silent shares the guilt. Verse 26 adds that he will speak only what he is given.

passages.title: A model siege reaches the prophet's body
passages.summary: God tells Ezekiel to draw Jerusalem on a clay brick. He must set up a model siege around it. He lies on his left side for 390 days for Israel’s guilt. Then he lies on his right side for forty days for Judah’s. He eats bread made from mixed grains, weighed out each day. He drinks a measured amount of water. He protests at cooking over human waste, and God allows cow dung. God says he will cut off Jerusalem’s supply of bread.

lds.text: How do measured meals explain the coming siege?

contextNote.title: A model siege reaches the prophet's body
contextNote.text: Ezekiel does not only speak about the siege. For more than a year his own body lives on siege rations. His bread is weighed, and his water is measured (verses 10–11). The mixed grains of verse 9 suggest the last scraps of a store. Verse 16 explains the sign. Jerusalem will eat by weight and drink in fear. Verse 14 records the priest’s protest, and verse 15 grants a change.

passages.title: Divided hair shows different forms of loss
passages.summary: God tells Ezekiel to shave his head and beard with a sword. He weighs the hair into three parts. He burns one part inside the model city. He strikes one part with the sword and scatters one to the wind. He tucks a few hairs into his robe and burns some of those. God says this is Jerusalem, set among the nations. She rebelled more than the nations around her. A third die of hunger, a third by sword, and a third are scattered.

lds.text: Why do even the protected hairs face a further threat?

contextNote.title: Divided hair shows different forms of loss
contextNote.text: The law told priests not to shave their heads (Leviticus 21:5). Ezekiel the priest does so with a sword. The hair is weighed on scales, so the judgment is measured. Verse 12 explains the three parts: disease and hunger, sword, and scattering. Verses 3–4 add a detail about the few hairs kept in his robe. Some of those are burned as well. Being among the survivors is no guarantee.

passages.title: Ruined shrines become places of remembrance
passages.summary: God tells Ezekiel to speak against the mountains of Israel. A sword is coming on the hilltop shrines. Altars will be ruined, and the dead will lie before their idols. Yet God will leave some who escape the sword. Among the nations they will remember him. They will remember how their unfaithful hearts grieved him. They will hate what they did. Then they will know that he is the LORD.

lds.text: How does remembrance change the meaning of survival?

contextNote.title: Ruined shrines become places of remembrance
contextNote.text: Verse 9 says something unusual about God. He says he has been broken by their unfaithful hearts. The verse describes hurt as well as anger. It also gives survival a purpose. Those who escape will remember him and loathe their own acts. The chapter repeats “you will know that I am the LORD” four times. Surviving is meant to lead to knowing.

passages.title: Wealth loses its power when daily life breaks
passages.summary: God says the end has come on the four corners of the land. He will judge the people by their own ways. Violence has grown into a rod of wickedness. Buyers need not rejoice, and sellers need not mourn. The trumpet sounds, and no one goes to battle. The sword is outside, and disease and hunger are inside. People throw their silver into the streets. Prophet, priest, and king have no help to give.

lds.text: Why can silver no longer provide the security its owners expected?

contextNote.title: Wealth loses its power when daily life breaks
contextNote.text: Verses 12–13 describe a market that has lost its meaning. Buying and selling land no longer matters. Verse 19 then says what happens to money. People throw it away as something unclean. It cannot rescue them, and it cannot feed them. The verse calls their wealth their stumbling block. Verse 20 explains: they made their gold into idols.

passages.title: A vision exposes what elders claim is hidden
passages.summary: Ezekiel sits with Judah’s elders in his house in Babylon. A fiery figure lifts him in a vision to Jerusalem’s temple. He sees an idol at the north gate. He digs through a wall and finds seventy elders burning incense to pictures of animals. They say the LORD does not see them. He sees women weeping for the god Tammuz. He sees twenty-five men bowing to the sun with their backs to the temple. God says they have filled the land with violence.

lds.text: How does the vision answer the elders’ claim that God cannot see?

contextNote.title: A vision exposes what elders claim is hidden
contextNote.text: The elders in verse 12 hold two beliefs. The LORD does not see, and he has left the land. The vision itself answers the first. God shows Ezekiel what they do in the dark, each in his own room. The second belief is nearly true, for a reason they miss. Verse 6 says their acts are driving him from his sanctuary. The chapter moves through four scenes, each called worse than the last.

passages.title: Grief distinguishes people within the city
passages.summary: God calls six men with weapons and one man in linen with a writing kit. The glory of God moves to the temple’s threshold. The man in linen must mark those who grieve over the city’s wrongs. The others are to strike everyone without the mark. They must begin at the sanctuary. Ezekiel falls on his face and asks whether God will destroy all who remain. God answers that the land is full of blood. The man in linen reports that he has done his task.

lds.text: Why does the vision distinguish mourners from other inhabitants?

contextNote.title: Grief distinguishes people within the city
contextNote.text: Verse 4 says who receives the protecting mark. They are people who sigh and cry over what is done in the city. They could not stop it, and they did not accept it. Grief is what sets them apart. Verse 6 says the judgment begins at the sanctuary, with the elders. Ezekiel pleads for the people in verse 8. He does not watch in silence.

passages.title: The glory leaves the sanctuary in stages
passages.summary: Ezekiel sees the sapphire throne above the cherubim again. The man in linen takes burning coals from between the wheels. He is to scatter them over the city. The cloud fills the inner court, and the glory rises to the threshold. Ezekiel describes the wheels and the four-faced creatures once more. He knows them as the creatures he saw by the river in Babylon. The glory leaves the threshold and rests above the cherubim. They rise and stop at the east gate.

lds.text: How does this departure connect with Ezekiel’s opening vision?

contextNote.title: The glory leaves the sanctuary in stages
contextNote.text: The glory leaves the temple in steps. It moves from the inner room to the threshold (9:3). In verse 18 it moves from the threshold to the cherubim. Verse 19 takes it to the east gate, and 11:23 to the hill beyond. The slow exit reads like reluctance. Verses 15 and 20 say these are the creatures Ezekiel saw in Babylon. What leaves Jerusalem is what appeared among the exiles.

passages.title: The exiles receive a promise denied by city leaders
passages.summary: At the east gate Ezekiel sees twenty-five leaders who give wicked advice. They say the city is a pot and they are the meat safe inside. God says he will bring them out and judge them. One of them dies while Ezekiel speaks. The people of Jerusalem say the exiles are far from the LORD. God answers that he has been a sanctuary to the exiles. He will gather them and give them one heart and a new spirit. Then the glory leaves the city and stands on the eastern hill.

lds.text: Why do distant exiles receive a promise of God’s presence?

contextNote.title: The exiles receive a promise denied by city leaders
contextNote.text: Verse 15 quotes Jerusalem’s residents about the exiles. They are far from the LORD, and the land now belongs to those who stayed. Verse 16 gives God’s reply. He himself has been a sanctuary to the exiles for a while. His presence did not depend on the building. Verse 19 then promises them a new heart of flesh. The people written off as rejected receive the promise.

passages.title: The prophet's baggage challenges postponed warnings
passages.summary: God tells Ezekiel to pack bags for exile while the people watch. In the evening he digs through the wall and carries his bag out. He covers his face so that he cannot see the land. He tells the people he is a sign for them. Their prince will leave in the dark and be taken to Babylon without seeing it. Ezekiel must eat his bread trembling. People say that visions never come true or concern the distant future. God says none of his words will be delayed any longer.

lds.text: How does the baggage make a postponed warning immediate?

contextNote.title: The prophet's baggage challenges postponed warnings
contextNote.text: Ezekiel acts first and explains only when asked (verse 9). Verse 11 gives the meaning: “I am your sign.” What he did will be done to them. The chapter quotes two sayings of the people. One says every vision fails (verse 22). The other says the vision is for a time far off (verse 27). A man carrying exile baggage today answers both.

passages.title: False peace resembles a weak wall under plaster
passages.summary: God speaks against prophets who prophesy from their own minds. They are like foxes among ruins. They have not gone up to repair the gaps in the wall. They say “Peace” when there is no peace. The people build a weak wall, and these prophets cover it with whitewash. Rain, hail, and wind will bring it down. God also speaks against women who sell charms and hunt lives for bread. They discourage the righteous and encourage the wicked.

lds.text: Why does whitewashed wall imagery fit a false promise of peace?

contextNote.title: False peace resembles a weak wall under plaster
contextNote.text: Verse 5 says what a prophet should do. He should stand in the gap and repair the wall. Verse 10 shows what these prophets do. The people put up a thin wall of their own hopes. The prophets paint it white so that it looks sound. Verse 11 says a storm will test it. Verse 22 names the damage: the righteous lose heart and the wicked do not turn.

passages.title: Another person's righteousness cannot replace one's own response
passages.summary: Some of Israel’s elders come and sit before Ezekiel. God says they have set up idols in their hearts. He asks whether such men should receive an answer. He calls the people to turn from their idols. Then he describes a land that sins and is struck by famine. Even Noah, Daniel, and Job could save only themselves there. They could not save a son or a daughter. Yet some survivors will come out, and their conduct will explain the judgment.

lds.text: Why cannot the three righteous figures rescue everyone else?

contextNote.title: Another person's righteousness cannot replace one's own response
contextNote.text: Verse 14 names three men known for righteousness. In their own stories each one helped others. Noah’s family entered the ark with him, and Job prayed for his friends. Here they could rescue no one else. Verses 16, 18, and 20 repeat it: not even sons or daughters. A person cannot rest on someone else’s goodness. The point is made four times, once for each disaster.

passages.title: The burned vine offers no useful timber
passages.summary: God asks Ezekiel how vine wood is better than any other wood. No one makes anything from it. No one even takes a peg from it to hang a pot. It is thrown on the fire as fuel. Both ends are burned, and the middle is charred. It was useless whole, and it is more useless burned. God says the people of Jerusalem are like that vine wood. He will give them to the fire.

lds.text: Why does this vine comparison focus on wood instead of fruit?

contextNote.title: The burned vine offers no useful timber
contextNote.text: Israel is often called a vine and praised for its fruit (Psalm 80:8–11). Ezekiel says nothing about fruit. He asks only about the wood. Vine wood is soft and twisted and makes nothing useful. A vine that bears no fruit has nothing else to offer. Verse 4 says the fire has already burned both ends. The short parable removes any pride in being God’s vine.

passages.title: Jerusalem's story overturns its claims of superiority
passages.summary: God tells Ezekiel to show Jerusalem her history. She was an unwanted baby left in a field. God said, “Live,” and later married her and dressed her as a queen. She trusted her beauty and gave herself to other gods and nations. She even sacrificed her children. Her sisters Samaria and Sodom did less wrong than she did. Sodom was proud and well fed and did not help the poor. Yet God will remember his covenant and forgive her.

lds.text: How does the comparison with Sodom challenge Jerusalem’s pride?

contextNote.title: Jerusalem's story overturns its claims of superiority
contextNote.text: Verse 49 defines Sodom’s guilt in social terms. She had pride, plenty of food, and easy comfort. She did not help the poor and needy. Verses 48 and 51 say Jerusalem has done worse. The comparison takes away her sense of being better. Verse 53 goes further and promises to restore Sodom too. The mercy of verses 60–63 is meant to leave her humbled.

passages.title: The eagles explain a broken royal oath
passages.summary: God gives Ezekiel a riddle about two eagles and a vine. A great eagle takes the top of a cedar and plants a seed. The seed becomes a low vine that grows toward him. Then the vine stretches its roots toward a second eagle. God explains that Babylon’s king took Judah’s king away. He made a treaty with a new king, who swore an oath. That king rebelled and sent to Egypt for horses. God will plant a tender shoot himself, and it will become a great cedar.

lds.text: Why does the vine’s search for another eagle become a broken obligation?

contextNote.title: The eagles explain a broken royal oath
contextNote.text: The first eagle is Babylon, and the second is Egypt. Judah’s king swore loyalty to Babylon and then turned to Egypt. Verse 15 asks whether a man who breaks a covenant can escape. Second Chronicles 36:13 says the oath was sworn by God. In verse 19 God calls it “my oath.” A promise made to a foreign conqueror still bound the king. Verses 22–24 end with a tree that God plants himself.

passages.title: Responsibility allows a changed future
passages.summary: The people quote a proverb: the fathers ate sour grapes, and the children’s teeth ache. God says they will not use it any more. Every life belongs to him, and the one who sins will die. A righteous man will live. His violent son will die for his own acts. That man’s son, if he does right, will live. A wicked person who turns will live, and his wrongs will not be remembered. God says he takes no pleasure in anyone’s death.

lds.text: How do the three generations challenge the sour-grapes saying?

contextNote.title: Responsibility allows a changed future
contextNote.text: The exiles used the proverb to say their fate was fixed by their parents. Verses 5–18 answer with three generations. A good father, a violent son, and a good grandson each stand alone. Verses 21–24 apply the same rule within one life. A person’s past does not lock his future. Verse 23 states what God wants. He would have the wicked turn and live.

passages.title: Royal power becomes a funeral song
passages.summary: Ezekiel sings a funeral song for the princes of Israel. Their mother was a lioness who raised her cubs. One cub became a young lion and was caught and taken to Egypt. Another prowled among the lions and was caged and taken to Babylon. Their mother was also like a vine with strong branches. It was pulled up in anger and planted in the desert. Fire came out from its own branch. No strong branch is left to be a ruler’s scepter.

lds.text: Why does the song combine royal strength with capture and burning?

contextNote.title: Royal power becomes a funeral song
contextNote.text: This is a funeral song sung while the royal house still stands. The lion recalls Jacob’s blessing on Judah in Genesis 49:9. The vine once grew strong branches fit for scepters (verse 11). Verse 14 says fire came from the vine’s own branch. The ruin begins inside the royal family. No branch remains that could rule. The verse says twice that this is a lament.

passages.title: The elders hear a history of repeated refusal
passages.summary: Elders come to Ezekiel to ask something of the LORD. God refuses to be consulted by them. He tells Ezekiel to recount their fathers’ history. In Egypt, in the desert, and in the land, Israel rebelled. Each time God held back for the sake of his name. The people now think they will be like the nations and serve wood and stone. God says that will never happen. He will rule them, purge the rebels, and bring them to his holy mountain.

lds.text: Why does this history repeat God’s concern for his name?

contextNote.title: The elders hear a history of repeated refusal
contextNote.text: Verse 32 exposes what the elders have in mind. They want to become like the nations around them. God says it “will not be at all.” He will not let them go. The history in this chapter turns four times on one phrase. God acted “for my name’s sake” (verses 9, 14, 22, 44). Israel’s story continues because of his name, and they do not earn it.

passages.title: A foreign ruler's choice becomes part of judgment
passages.summary: God says his sword is drawn against Jerusalem, and Ezekiel must groan aloud. The sword is sharpened and polished. Ezekiel marks out two roads for the king of Babylon. One leads to the Ammonite capital and one to Jerusalem. The king stops at the fork and uses arrows, idols, and a liver to decide. The lot falls on Jerusalem. Judah’s prince must take off his crown. It will be given to the one who has the right to it.

lds.text: Why does dismissing the foreign ruler’s choice fail to protect Jerusalem?

contextNote.title: A foreign ruler's choice becomes part of judgment
contextNote.text: Verse 21 lists three ways of seeking omens. Deuteronomy 18:10 forbids such practices in Israel. Yet the lot points where God has already said the sword will go. A foreign king’s superstition becomes part of the judgment. Verse 23 says the people of Jerusalem think the omen is false. Their doubt does not protect them. Verse 27 keeps the crown for a future rightful ruler.

passages.title: The city's wrongs involve every level of power
passages.summary: God calls Jerusalem a city of bloodshed. Its princes use their power to kill. People dishonor parents and wrong the foreigner, the orphan, and the widow. They take bribes and interest and have forgotten God. Israel has become like the waste left when metal is melted. Prophets, priests, and officials all devour the people. The common people also rob the poor and the foreigner. God looked for one person to stand in the gap and found none.

lds.text: How do abuses against poor people connect with failures in worship?

contextNote.title: The city's wrongs involve every level of power
contextNote.text: Verses 25–29 go through the city by rank. Prophets, priests, and officials are charged first. Verse 29 then names “the people of the land.” Ordinary people also oppress the poor and the foreigner. No class is left out. Wrongs against the weak appear beside wrongs against holy things (verses 7–8). Verse 30 says God searched for one person to repair the wall.

passages.title: The sisters represent cities and dangerous alliances
passages.summary: God tells a story of two sisters, Samaria and Jerusalem. Both were unfaithful from their youth in Egypt. Samaria desired the Assyrians and was handed over to them. Jerusalem saw this and did worse. She desired the Assyrians and then the Babylonians. God will bring those lovers against her as attackers. She must drink her sister’s cup of ruin. The sisters are charged with idolatry and with sacrificing their children.

lds.text: What changes when the cities’ desired allies become their attackers?

contextNote.title: The sisters represent cities and dangerous alliances
contextNote.text: The sisters stand for two capital cities and their foreign alliances. Each was drawn to a great power’s strength and display. Verse 22 says the admired allies will return as enemies. Verse 37 states the actual charges under the picture. The cities worshiped idols and burned their own children. Verse 39 adds that they entered God’s house that same day. The harsh language is aimed at cities and their politics.

passages.title: Public signs join the city's siege with private grief
passages.summary: On the day Babylon’s siege begins, God tells Ezekiel to record the date. He gives a parable of a cooking pot that cannot be cleaned. Then God says he will take away the delight of Ezekiel’s eyes. Ezekiel must not mourn or weep. His wife dies that evening, and he does as he was told. The people ask what this means for them. God says he will take his sanctuary, the delight of their eyes. They will be too stunned to mourn, as Ezekiel was.

lds.text: Why do the people ask about Ezekiel’s unusual response to loss?

contextNote.title: Public signs join the city's siege with private grief
contextNote.text: Verse 16 calls Ezekiel’s wife the desire of his eyes. Verse 21 uses the same words for the temple. What she is to him, the sanctuary is to the people. His silence at her death shows what their grief will be like. The loss will be too great for the usual rites (verses 22–23). The text gives the prophet’s own cost one line in verse 18. It moves at once to the people’s question.

passages.title: The neighbors face judgment for celebrating another people's loss
passages.summary: God speaks against four neighbors of Judah. Ammon gloated when the temple was profaned and Judah went into exile. Ammon clapped, stamped, and rejoiced with contempt. Moab said Judah was like every other nation. Edom took revenge on Judah. The Philistines acted with old hatred. God will hand Ammon and Moab to the peoples of the east. He will lay his hand on Edom and the Philistines.

lds.text: Why does celebrating Judah’s loss become a charge against its neighbors?

contextNote.title: The neighbors face judgment for celebrating another people's loss
contextNote.text: None of these nations is charged with idolatry here. Verse 6 charges Ammon with clapping and stamping for joy. They celebrated another people’s ruin. Each neighbor shows a different attitude. Moab denies that Judah was special (verse 8), and Edom takes revenge (verse 12). The Philistines act from long hatred (verse 15). God judged Judah, and that gave its neighbors no right to rejoice.

passages.title: Tyre's expected gain becomes a warning of loss
passages.summary: God speaks against the trading city of Tyre. Tyre gloated when Jerusalem fell. It expected to grow rich now that a rival gate was broken. God will bring many nations against it like waves. Nebuchadnezzar will come with horses, chariots, and siege works. Tyre’s wealth and goods will be plundered. Its stones and timber will be thrown into the sea. The rulers of the coast will tremble and sing a lament.

lds.text: How does hoped-for profit from Jerusalem’s fall reverse in the warning?

contextNote.title: Tyre's expected gain becomes a warning of loss
contextNote.text: Verse 2 gives Tyre’s reaction to Jerusalem’s fall. A trade rival is gone, so Tyre expects more business. The warning reverses that hope point by point. Verse 12 says Tyre’s own riches and goods will be taken. Its fine houses will be torn down. Verses 4 and 14 leave only bare rock for drying nets. The profit it expected from another’s loss becomes its own loss.

passages.title: A trading city becomes a richly equipped ship
passages.summary: God tells Ezekiel to sing a lament for Tyre. The city is pictured as a beautiful ship. Its planks, mast, oars, and sail come from many lands. Men of many nations row it and guard it. A long list names its trading partners and their goods. The cargo includes metals, horses, ivory, wheat, wine, and slaves. An east wind breaks the ship in the heart of the sea. Sailors and merchants weep at its fall.

lds.text: How does the list of trading partners increase the scale of loss?

contextNote.title: A trading city becomes a richly equipped ship
contextNote.text: Verses 5–7 build the ship from the best materials of every coast. Verses 12–25 list its trade, nation by nation. The list shows how many peoples depended on this one city. Verse 13 includes human beings among the goods. Verse 27 then sinks everything in a single sentence. Wealth, wares, sailors, and soldiers go down together. The length of the list measures the size of the loss.

passages.title: Royal splendor cannot make a ruler divine
passages.summary: God speaks to the ruler of Tyre, who says he is a god. He is a man, though he is wise and has grown rich. Foreigners will kill him, and he will not claim to be a god then. A lament follows for the king of Tyre. He was in Eden, covered with precious stones. He was blameless until wrong was found in him. Trade filled him with violence, and beauty made him proud. A short message then promises Israel a safe home.

lds.text: Why does the ruler’s wealth fail to support his claim to divinity?

contextNote.title: Royal splendor cannot make a ruler divine
contextNote.text: Verse 2 quotes the ruler’s claim to sit in God’s seat. Verse 9 asks whether he will say so in front of his killers. Verses 16–17 trace how he fell. Much trade led to violence. Beauty lifted his heart, and splendor spoiled his wisdom. The Eden language makes him like Adam, favored and then cast out. Some Christian readers also see Satan’s fall here, but the text names Tyre’s king.

passages.title: Egypt's river cannot belong to Pharaoh alone
passages.summary: God speaks against Pharaoh, the great monster lying in the Nile. Pharaoh says the river is his and he made it. God will put hooks in his jaws and leave him in the desert. Egypt was a reed staff that broke when Israel leaned on it. The land will be desolate for forty years. Then Egypt will return as a lowly kingdom. A later message says Nebuchadnezzar got no wages from Tyre. God will give him Egypt as his pay.

lds.text: How does the later speech distinguish effort against Tyre from expected payment?

contextNote.title: Egypt's river cannot belong to Pharaoh alone
contextNote.text: The Nile was Egypt’s life, and verse 9 quotes Pharaoh’s claim about it. He says the river is his and that he made it. That is a creator’s claim. Verse 3 pictures him as a great river beast. Verses 6–7 add a second charge. Egypt was a reed that splintered when Israel leaned on it. Verses 14–15 leave Egypt alive and too small to be trusted again.

passages.title: Egypt's strength fails across cities and allies
passages.summary: God says a day of clouds is near for Egypt. The sword will come, and Egypt’s allies will fall with it. Nebuchadnezzar will destroy the land. God will end the idols of Memphis and judge Egypt’s cities by name. At Tahpanhes the day will grow dark. A second message says God has broken Pharaoh’s arm. It has not been bound up to hold a sword. God will strengthen the arms of Babylon’s king.

lds.text: What does the broken-arm comparison say about expected military help?

contextNote.title: Egypt's strength fails across cities and allies
contextNote.text: Verses 13–18 name Egypt’s cities from one end to the other. No region is passed over. Verse 18 ends at Tahpanhes. Judah’s refugees fled to that town with Jeremiah (Jeremiah 43:7–9). The verse says Egypt’s “yokes” will be broken there. Verses 21–25 add the picture of a broken arm. The ally Judah counted on cannot lift a sword.

passages.title: A great tree warns Pharaoh about exalted power
passages.summary: God asks Pharaoh whom he resembles in his greatness. Assyria was a cedar of Lebanon, taller than every tree. Deep waters fed it, and birds nested in its branches. All great nations lived in its shade. Because it grew proud of its height, God gave it to a ruthless nation. Foreigners cut it down, and its branches fell on the hills. It went down to the grave. Pharaoh and his many people will be brought down the same way.

lds.text: Why does Pharaoh hear a warning through another power’s tree?

contextNote.title: A great tree warns Pharaoh about exalted power
contextNote.text: Pharaoh hears his warning through the story of another empire. Assyria had been greater than Egypt, and it had already fallen. Verse 6 shows the tree doing good. Birds nested in it, and nations lived in its shade. Verse 10 names the fault: its heart was lifted up because of its height. Verse 14 gives the lesson for every tall tree. None should exalt itself, since all are headed for death.

passages.title: The funeral song places Egypt beside fallen powers
passages.summary: Ezekiel sings a lament for Pharaoh. He thought himself a lion, but he is a monster that muddies the rivers. God will catch him in a net and darken the sky over him. Then Ezekiel is told to wail for Egypt’s crowds. They go down to the pit with other fallen nations. Assyria is there, and Elam, Meshech, Tubal, Edom, and the Sidonians. Each once spread terror in the land of the living. Pharaoh will see them and be consoled over his own army.

lds.text: How does shared burial reverse the nations’ former terror?

contextNote.title: The funeral song places Egypt beside fallen powers
contextNote.text: Verse 18 sends Egypt down to join other great powers. The verses that follow read like a roll call. Each nation “caused terror in the land of the living.” Each now lies still and bears its shame. The phrase returns again and again (verses 23–27, 32). Egypt takes its place among equals. Verse 31 gives Pharaoh one comfort: he is not alone there.

passages.title: Hearing the warning is different from acting on it
passages.summary: God again makes Ezekiel a watchman for Israel. The people say their sins weigh on them and they are wasting away. God says he takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked. A wicked person who turns and makes things right will live. A man escapes from Jerusalem and reports that the city has fallen. Those left in the ruins claim the land, and God rejects their claim. The exiles now come to hear Ezekiel. They listen as to a love song and do not act.

lds.text: The lesson studies repentance as a change of conduct that can lead to life. Why does enjoying the prophet’s voice fail to answer his message?

contextNote.title: Hearing the warning is different from acting on it
contextNote.text: After Jerusalem falls, Ezekiel is proved right, and people come to him. Verse 30 shows them inviting one another to hear the word. Verse 31 says they sit, listen, and do nothing. Their mouths show love, and their hearts chase gain. Verse 32 compares the prophet to a singer with a fine voice. An audience that enjoys him has not obeyed him. Verse 33 says events will show that a prophet was among them.

passages.title: The shepherd must repair harm and prevent further abuse
passages.summary: God speaks against Israel’s shepherds, who feed themselves. They do not strengthen the weak, heal the sick, or search for the lost. The flock is scattered and has become food for wild animals. God says he himself will search for his sheep. He will bring them home and feed them on good pasture. He will also judge between one sheep and another. The strong have shoved the weak and fouled the water. He will set one shepherd over them, his servant David.

lds.text: The lesson connects the shepherd’s care with following the Savior. Why must care for wounded sheep include judgment against stronger sheep?

contextNote.title: The shepherd must repair harm and prevent further abuse
contextNote.text: Verse 4 lists what the shepherds failed to do. Verse 16 takes up that list item by item. God will seek the lost, bind the injured, and strengthen the sick. The verse then adds a judgment on the fat and strong. Verses 17–22 explain it. Some sheep push the weak aside and muddy the water. Care for the hurt includes restraint of those who hurt them.

passages.title: Seir's claim to the land meets God's continuing presence
passages.summary: God tells Ezekiel to speak against Mount Seir, the land of Edom. Edom kept an old hatred and gave Israelites to the sword in their disaster. So bloodshed will pursue Edom. Edom said the two nations and their lands would be its own. Yet the LORD was there. God heard every insult Edom spoke against Israel’s mountains. Edom rejoiced when Israel’s land lay empty. Its own land will be made empty.

lds.text: How does God’s presence challenge Seir’s claim to empty land?

contextNote.title: Seir's claim to the land meets God's continuing presence
contextNote.text: After the exile, the lands of Israel and Judah looked empty. Verse 10 quotes Edom’s plan to take both. The verse then adds one clause: “although the LORD was there.” The land appeared abandoned, and its owner had not given it up. Edom’s claim ignored him. Verse 13 says Edom’s boasting was aimed at God. The next chapter speaks to those same mountains with a promise.

passages.title: A restored land requires a changed people
passages.summary: God speaks to the mountains of Israel. Enemies have claimed them, and they will soon bear fruit for his people. Israel defiled the land and was scattered among the nations. There the people brought dishonor on God’s name. He will act for the sake of that name and bring them home. He will sprinkle clean water on them. He will give them a new heart and put his Spirit in them. The ruined land will become like the garden of Eden.
passages.uncertainty: This chapter has no mapped places. Visionary settings and uncertain river locations remain unmapped.

lds.text: The lesson connects a new heart with repentance and obedience. Why does return require more than new homes and productive fields?

contextNote.title: A restored land requires a changed people
contextNote.text: The promise comes in a set order. God gathers the people (verse 24) and cleanses them (verse 25). Then he gives a new heart (verse 26) and his Spirit (verse 27). Obedience follows from that. A heart of stone does not respond; a heart of flesh does. Without that change a return would only repeat the past (verses 17–19). Verses 22 and 32 say he does this for his name, not their merit.

passages.title: Revived bones and joined sticks answer divided hope
passages.summary: The LORD sets Ezekiel in a valley full of dry bones. He asks whether the bones can live, and Ezekiel says only God knows. Ezekiel speaks, and the bones join and are covered with flesh. He speaks again, and breath enters them, and they stand. God says the bones are the whole house of Israel. He will bring them out of their graves to their land. Ezekiel joins two sticks marked for Judah and Joseph. God will make them one nation under one king.

lds.text: The lesson also reads the sticks as the Bible and the Book of Mormon. This later Church interpretation differs from Ezekiel’s explanation of reunited peoples. Doctrine and Covenants 27:5 speaks of the record of the stick of Ephraim. How do the bones and sticks answer different forms of separation?

contextNote.title: Revived bones and joined sticks answer divided hope
contextNote.text: Verse 11 quotes what the exiles are saying. Their bones are dry, their hope is gone, and they are cut off. The vision answers that saying. It happens in two stages (verses 7–10). The bodies are formed first and have no breath. Life comes only when the breath enters, as in Genesis 2:7. The two sticks in verses 16–22 then promise one reunited people.

passages.title: A secure people become the target of planned plunder
passages.summary: God speaks against Gog, a ruler from the far north. Gog leads a great army with many allies. In later years he will invade a land restored from war. Its people will be living safely in villages without walls. Gog plans to seize plunder from them. Merchants ask whether he has come for silver and gold. God says he will bring Gog there so that the nations may know him. Earthquake, sword, hail, and fire will meet the army.

lds.text: Why does the attacker treat peaceful villages as an opportunity?

contextNote.title: A secure people become the target of planned plunder
contextNote.text: Verse 11 gives Gog’s reasoning. The villages have no walls, bars, or gates. Their people are at rest and suspect nothing. He sees their peace as an opening. Verse 13 shows traders watching for a share of the loot. Verse 16 states God’s purpose in letting him come. The nations will learn who guards a people with no walls.

passages.title: The invader's weapons become fuel instead of power
passages.summary: God says Gog will fall on the mountains of Israel. Birds and wild animals will feed on his army. Israel will burn the invaders’ weapons as fuel for seven years. They will bury the dead for seven months to cleanse the land. The nations will learn that Israel went into exile for its own sin. God hid his face from them then. Now he will restore Jacob and have mercy. He will pour out his Spirit and hide his face no more.

lds.text: How do fuel and burial work reverse the invader’s display of strength?

contextNote.title: The invader's weapons become fuel instead of power
contextNote.text: Verses 9–10 turn the invaders’ weapons into firewood. Verses 12–16 turn their army into a long burial task. Tools of terror become household fuel and a cleanup job. Verse 22 gives the result for Israel: they will know the LORD. Verse 23 gives the result for the nations. They will learn that the exile came from Israel’s guilt, not God’s weakness. Verse 29 ends with his face no longer hidden.

passages.title: A measured vision prepares the people to see again
passages.summary: In the twenty-fifth year of exile, God brings Ezekiel in a vision to Israel. On a high mountain he sees buildings like a city. A man who shines like bronze holds a measuring rod. He tells Ezekiel to look, listen, and pay close attention. He measures the outer wall and the east gate with its guardrooms. He measures the outer court and its other gates. He measures the inner court and the tables for offerings. He names the rooms for the priests who serve.

lds.text: Why does the guide require careful looking and listening before reporting?

contextNote.title: A measured vision prepares the people to see again
contextNote.text: Verse 1 dates this vision fourteen years after the city fell. The exiles have no temple. Verse 4 gives Ezekiel three commands: see, hear, and set his heart. Then he must report everything to Israel. The guide measures, and Ezekiel watches and records. Exact sizes make the future house solid in the hearers’ minds. Nine chapters of measurements are a form of hope.

passages.title: The inner rooms give sacred space a clear order
passages.summary: The guide brings Ezekiel into the main hall of the temple and measures it. He goes alone into the inner room and measures it. He says, “This is the most holy place.” Side rooms stand in three stories around the house. A large building lies to the west. The walls are paneled with wood and carved with cherubim and palm trees. Each cherub has a human face and a lion’s face. A wooden altar stands before the inner room.

lds.text: How do different entrances mark the movement toward the most holy place?

contextNote.title: The inner rooms give sacred space a clear order
contextNote.text: The guide speaks very little in these chapters. Verse 4 is one of the few things he says. He names the inner room. Verse 3 notes that he “went inward” to measure it. Ezekiel is a priest, and he stays outside. The doorways grow narrower toward that room (verses 2–3). The building’s plan teaches that nearness to God has steps.

passages.title: Priestly rooms protect the distinction between sacred and common
passages.summary: The guide shows Ezekiel two blocks of rooms beside the temple. They stand three stories high with walkways in front. Priests who come near the LORD eat the most holy offerings there. They store the offerings in those rooms. They must leave their service clothes there before going to the outer court. They put on other clothes to go where the people are. The guide then measures the whole area. A wall around it separates the holy from the common.

lds.text: Why must priests change garments before approaching the people’s area?

contextNote.title: Priestly rooms protect the distinction between sacred and common
contextNote.text: Verse 14 gives a rule about clothing. Garments worn in service stay in the holy rooms. The priests change before they go out among the people. Holiness is treated as something not to be carried about carelessly. Verse 20 states the purpose of the whole outer wall. It marks off the holy from the common. Chapter 22:26 charged the earlier priests with ignoring that difference.

passages.title: The returning glory requires distance from former wrongs
passages.summary: The guide brings Ezekiel to the east gate. The glory of Israel’s God comes from the east with a sound like rushing water. Ezekiel knows it as the glory he saw before, and he falls on his face. The glory enters the temple and fills it. A voice says this is the place of God’s throne. He will live there among Israel forever. The people must put away their old defilements. Ezekiel then receives the measurements and rites of the altar.

lds.text: How does the return of glory answer its earlier departure?

contextNote.title: The returning glory requires distance from former wrongs
contextNote.text: The glory left by the east gate in 10:19 and 11:23. It returns by that same gate in verse 4. Verse 3 ties this sight to the earlier visions. Verse 7 says God will live here forever, and it sets a condition. The people must no longer defile his name. Verse 8 recalls kings who built beside his house with only a wall between. Verses 10–11 say the plan itself should make Israel ashamed.

passages.title: Priests must teach the distinctions they once failed to keep
passages.summary: The east gate stays shut, since the LORD has entered by it. Only the prince may sit there to eat. God rebukes Israel for letting unfaithful foreigners serve in his house. Levites who went after idols may serve only as gatekeepers and helpers. The sons of Zadok, who stayed faithful, will come near as priests. They wear linen, trim their hair, and drink no wine before serving. They must teach the people the difference between holy and common. They own no land, for God is their inheritance.

lds.text: How does the teaching duty answer the earlier charge against priests?

contextNote.title: Priests must teach the distinctions they once failed to keep
contextNote.text: Chapter 22:26 accused the priests of teaching no difference between holy and common. Verse 23 answers that charge. The restored priests must teach exactly that difference. They must also help people tell clean from unclean. Verse 24 adds that they judge disputes by God’s rules. Their own habits of dress and conduct model the lesson (verses 17–22). Verse 28 says God himself is what they own.

passages.title: Land and honest measures restrain royal abuse
passages.summary: The land is to be divided, with a holy district set apart for the LORD. It holds the sanctuary and land for priests and Levites. The city receives its own portion. The prince receives land on both sides of the holy district. God tells the princes to stop their violence and stop evicting his people. They must use honest scales and honest measures. The people bring set offerings to the prince. He provides the sacrifices at feasts and Sabbaths.

lds.text: Why do assigned royal land and honest measures belong together?

contextNote.title: Land and honest measures restrain royal abuse
contextNote.text: Verses 7–8 give the prince a fixed estate with marked borders. He has his own land and no reason to take another’s. Verse 9 then speaks sharply: “Enough, you princes of Israel!” It names violence, plunder, and driving people from their homes. First Kings 21 shows a king taking Naboth’s vineyard. Verses 10–12 add honest weights and measures. Seizing land and cheating in trade are treated as one kind of wrong.

passages.title: The prince's family gifts must not displace other households
passages.summary: The inner east gate opens on Sabbaths and new moons. The prince worships at the threshold of the gate and does not go farther. The people worship at the entrance. At the feasts each person leaves by the gate opposite the one he entered. The prince goes in and out among them. A lamb is offered every morning. The prince may give land to his sons only from his own estate. The chapter ends with the kitchens where offerings are cooked.

lds.text: How does the inheritance rule restrain the prince’s power?

contextNote.title: The prince's family gifts must not displace other households
contextNote.text: Verses 16–17 limit what a prince may give away. Land given to his sons stays in his family. Land given to a servant returns in the year of release. Verse 18 states the rule beneath both. He may not take the people’s inheritance to enrich his house. The reason given is that no one be driven from his property. Verse 10 has the prince enter and leave with the people.

passages.title: Life from the sanctuary reaches land shared with foreigners
passages.summary: Water flows from under the temple’s threshold toward the east. The guide measures it four times, and it deepens from ankle to a river. Trees grow thick on both banks. The water runs down to the Dead Sea and makes it fresh. Fish swarm there, and fishermen spread their nets. The trees bear fruit every month, and their leaves heal. God then gives the borders of the land. Foreigners who settle there receive an inheritance with the tribes.

lds.text: The lesson reads the healing river through blessings associated with temple worship. How does inheritance for resident foreigners extend the promise of restored life?

contextNote.title: Life from the sanctuary reaches land shared with foreigners
contextNote.text: The river starts as a trickle and grows with no streams joining (verses 3–5). It heals the most lifeless water in the land (verses 8–9). Verse 22 then turns to who may own the renewed land. Foreigners who live there and raise children receive a share. They are to be treated as native-born Israelites. Leviticus 19:34 told Israel to love the foreigner. This verse gives the foreigner land.

passages.title: The city's final name completes the promise of presence
passages.summary: The land is divided among the tribes in strips from north to south. Seven tribes lie north of the holy district. The district holds the sanctuary, the priests, and the Levites. The city lies beside it, and workers from every tribe farm its land. The prince’s land lies on either side. Five tribes lie to the south. The city has twelve gates, each named for a tribe. From that day the city’s name is “The LORD is there.”

lds.text: Why does the book end by naming the city’s relationship with God?

contextNote.title: The city's final name completes the promise of presence
contextNote.text: Joshua’s division gave the tribes uneven shares. This one gives each tribe a strip of the same kind. The northern tribes lost in exile are all present. Each tribe has a gate into the city (verses 31–34). The book began with God’s glory seen in Babylon. It showed that glory leaving Jerusalem. Verse 35 ends with a city renamed for his presence.

events.title: God's glory appears among the exiles
events.summary: Ezekiel is a priest living among the exiles by a river in Babylon. The heavens open, and he sees visions of God. A storm comes from the north with flashing fire. In it are four living creatures, each with four faces and four wings. Beside each is a wheel within a wheel, full of eyes. Above them is a shining platform and a throne like sapphire. On the throne is a figure like a man, surrounded by fire and a rainbow. Ezekiel falls on his face and hears a voice.
events.detail: The vision comes in Babylon, far from the temple. The throne has wheels that move in any direction (verse 17). So God’s presence is not fixed to one place. Verse 28 describes what Ezekiel saw with great caution. It was “the appearance of the likeness” of the LORD’s glory. He does not claim to describe God directly. The rainbow in the storm recalls the sign of mercy in Genesis 9:13.

lds.text: The 2026 lesson emphasizes God’s presence among exiles. Why does the glory appear among people far from Jerusalem?

events.title: Speaking does not depend on a willing audience
events.summary: A voice tells Ezekiel to stand on his feet. The Spirit enters him and sets him upright. God sends him to the people of Israel, a rebellious nation. He must say, “This is what the Lord GOD says.” Whether they listen or not, they will know a prophet was among them. He must not fear them, though they are like thorns and scorpions. He must not be rebellious as they are. A hand holds out a scroll full of mourning and woe.
events.detail: God calls Ezekiel “son of man,” which means a human being. The title follows directly on the vision of glory. Verse 2 says the Spirit had to set him on his feet. Verse 7 defines his task. He must speak whether the people hear or refuse. His success is not measured by their response. Verse 5 names the one sure result: they will know a prophet was there.

lds.text: The lesson’s opening invites people to hear God’s word. Why must Ezekiel speak even when his listeners refuse?

events.title: The messenger must hear before he warns
events.summary: Ezekiel eats the scroll, and it is as sweet as honey. God says foreigners would listen, but Israel will not. God makes his forehead as hard as flint. The Spirit carries him to the exiles, and he sits stunned for seven days. Then God makes him a watchman for Israel. If he fails to warn the wicked, he will answer for their blood. If he warns them, he has saved his own life. God then makes him unable to speak except when given a message.
events.detail: A watchman stood on the wall and warned of danger. Verse 17 puts hearing before warning. Ezekiel must first receive the word from God’s mouth. Verses 18–21 hold him responsible for giving the warning. They do not hold him responsible for the result. A watchman who keeps silent shares the guilt. Verse 26 adds that he will speak only what he is given.

events.title: A model siege reaches the prophet's body
events.summary: God tells Ezekiel to draw Jerusalem on a clay brick. He must set up a model siege around it. He lies on his left side for 390 days for Israel’s guilt. Then he lies on his right side for forty days for Judah’s. He eats bread made from mixed grains, weighed out each day. He drinks a measured amount of water. He protests at cooking over human waste, and God allows cow dung. God says he will cut off Jerusalem’s supply of bread.
events.detail: Ezekiel does not only speak about the siege. For more than a year his own body lives on siege rations. His bread is weighed, and his water is measured (verses 10–11). The mixed grains of verse 9 suggest the last scraps of a store. Verse 16 explains the sign. Jerusalem will eat by weight and drink in fear. Verse 14 records the priest’s protest, and verse 15 grants a change.

events.title: Divided hair shows different forms of loss
events.summary: God tells Ezekiel to shave his head and beard with a sword. He weighs the hair into three parts. He burns one part inside the model city. He strikes one part with the sword and scatters one to the wind. He tucks a few hairs into his robe and burns some of those. God says this is Jerusalem, set among the nations. She rebelled more than the nations around her. A third die of hunger, a third by sword, and a third are scattered.
events.detail: The law told priests not to shave their heads (Leviticus 21:5). Ezekiel the priest does so with a sword. The hair is weighed on scales, so the judgment is measured. Verse 12 explains the three parts: disease and hunger, sword, and scattering. Verses 3–4 add a detail about the few hairs kept in his robe. Some of those are burned as well. Being among the survivors is no guarantee.

events.title: Ruined shrines become places of remembrance
events.summary: God tells Ezekiel to speak against the mountains of Israel. A sword is coming on the hilltop shrines. Altars will be ruined, and the dead will lie before their idols. Yet God will leave some who escape the sword. Among the nations they will remember him. They will remember how their unfaithful hearts grieved him. They will hate what they did. Then they will know that he is the LORD.
events.detail: Verse 9 says something unusual about God. He says he has been broken by their unfaithful hearts. The verse describes hurt as well as anger. It also gives survival a purpose. Those who escape will remember him and loathe their own acts. The chapter repeats “you will know that I am the LORD” four times. Surviving is meant to lead to knowing.

events.title: Wealth loses its power when daily life breaks
events.summary: God says the end has come on the four corners of the land. He will judge the people by their own ways. Violence has grown into a rod of wickedness. Buyers need not rejoice, and sellers need not mourn. The trumpet sounds, and no one goes to battle. The sword is outside, and disease and hunger are inside. People throw their silver into the streets. Prophet, priest, and king have no help to give.
events.detail: Verses 12–13 describe a market that has lost its meaning. Buying and selling land no longer matters. Verse 19 then says what happens to money. People throw it away as something unclean. It cannot rescue them, and it cannot feed them. The verse calls their wealth their stumbling block. Verse 20 explains: they made their gold into idols.

events.title: A vision exposes what elders claim is hidden
events.summary: Ezekiel sits with Judah’s elders in his house in Babylon. A fiery figure lifts him in a vision to Jerusalem’s temple. He sees an idol at the north gate. He digs through a wall and finds seventy elders burning incense to pictures of animals. They say the LORD does not see them. He sees women weeping for the god Tammuz. He sees twenty-five men bowing to the sun with their backs to the temple. God says they have filled the land with violence.
events.detail: The elders in verse 12 hold two beliefs. The LORD does not see, and he has left the land. The vision itself answers the first. God shows Ezekiel what they do in the dark, each in his own room. The second belief is nearly true, for a reason they miss. Verse 6 says their acts are driving him from his sanctuary. The chapter moves through four scenes, each called worse than the last.

events.title: Grief distinguishes people within the city
events.summary: God calls six men with weapons and one man in linen with a writing kit. The glory of God moves to the temple’s threshold. The man in linen must mark those who grieve over the city’s wrongs. The others are to strike everyone without the mark. They must begin at the sanctuary. Ezekiel falls on his face and asks whether God will destroy all who remain. God answers that the land is full of blood. The man in linen reports that he has done his task.
events.detail: Verse 4 says who receives the protecting mark. They are people who sigh and cry over what is done in the city. They could not stop it, and they did not accept it. Grief is what sets them apart. Verse 6 says the judgment begins at the sanctuary, with the elders. Ezekiel pleads for the people in verse 8. He does not watch in silence.

events.title: The glory leaves the sanctuary in stages
events.summary: Ezekiel sees the sapphire throne above the cherubim again. The man in linen takes burning coals from between the wheels. He is to scatter them over the city. The cloud fills the inner court, and the glory rises to the threshold. Ezekiel describes the wheels and the four-faced creatures once more. He knows them as the creatures he saw by the river in Babylon. The glory leaves the threshold and rests above the cherubim. They rise and stop at the east gate.
events.detail: The glory leaves the temple in steps. It moves from the inner room to the threshold (9:3). In verse 18 it moves from the threshold to the cherubim. Verse 19 takes it to the east gate, and 11:23 to the hill beyond. The slow exit reads like reluctance. Verses 15 and 20 say these are the creatures Ezekiel saw in Babylon. What leaves Jerusalem is what appeared among the exiles.

events.title: The exiles receive a promise denied by city leaders
events.summary: At the east gate Ezekiel sees twenty-five leaders who give wicked advice. They say the city is a pot and they are the meat safe inside. God says he will bring them out and judge them. One of them dies while Ezekiel speaks. The people of Jerusalem say the exiles are far from the LORD. God answers that he has been a sanctuary to the exiles. He will gather them and give them one heart and a new spirit. Then the glory leaves the city and stands on the eastern hill.
events.detail: Verse 15 quotes Jerusalem’s residents about the exiles. They are far from the LORD, and the land now belongs to those who stayed. Verse 16 gives God’s reply. He himself has been a sanctuary to the exiles for a while. His presence did not depend on the building. Verse 19 then promises them a new heart of flesh. The people written off as rejected receive the promise.

events.title: The prophet's baggage challenges postponed warnings
events.summary: God tells Ezekiel to pack bags for exile while the people watch. In the evening he digs through the wall and carries his bag out. He covers his face so that he cannot see the land. He tells the people he is a sign for them. Their prince will leave in the dark and be taken to Babylon without seeing it. Ezekiel must eat his bread trembling. People say that visions never come true or concern the distant future. God says none of his words will be delayed any longer.
events.detail: Ezekiel acts first and explains only when asked (verse 9). Verse 11 gives the meaning: “I am your sign.” What he did will be done to them. The chapter quotes two sayings of the people. One says every vision fails (verse 22). The other says the vision is for a time far off (verse 27). A man carrying exile baggage today answers both.

events.title: False peace resembles a weak wall under plaster
events.summary: God speaks against prophets who prophesy from their own minds. They are like foxes among ruins. They have not gone up to repair the gaps in the wall. They say “Peace” when there is no peace. The people build a weak wall, and these prophets cover it with whitewash. Rain, hail, and wind will bring it down. God also speaks against women who sell charms and hunt lives for bread. They discourage the righteous and encourage the wicked.
events.detail: Verse 5 says what a prophet should do. He should stand in the gap and repair the wall. Verse 10 shows what these prophets do. The people put up a thin wall of their own hopes. The prophets paint it white so that it looks sound. Verse 11 says a storm will test it. Verse 22 names the damage: the righteous lose heart and the wicked do not turn.

events.title: Another person's righteousness cannot replace one's own response
events.summary: Some of Israel’s elders come and sit before Ezekiel. God says they have set up idols in their hearts. He asks whether such men should receive an answer. He calls the people to turn from their idols. Then he describes a land that sins and is struck by famine. Even Noah, Daniel, and Job could save only themselves there. They could not save a son or a daughter. Yet some survivors will come out, and their conduct will explain the judgment.
events.detail: Verse 14 names three men known for righteousness. In their own stories each one helped others. Noah’s family entered the ark with him, and Job prayed for his friends. Here they could rescue no one else. Verses 16, 18, and 20 repeat it: not even sons or daughters. A person cannot rest on someone else’s goodness. The point is made four times, once for each disaster.

events.title: The burned vine offers no useful timber
events.summary: God asks Ezekiel how vine wood is better than any other wood. No one makes anything from it. No one even takes a peg from it to hang a pot. It is thrown on the fire as fuel. Both ends are burned, and the middle is charred. It was useless whole, and it is more useless burned. God says the people of Jerusalem are like that vine wood. He will give them to the fire.
events.detail: Israel is often called a vine and praised for its fruit (Psalm 80:8–11). Ezekiel says nothing about fruit. He asks only about the wood. Vine wood is soft and twisted and makes nothing useful. A vine that bears no fruit has nothing else to offer. Verse 4 says the fire has already burned both ends. The short parable removes any pride in being God’s vine.

events.title: Jerusalem's story overturns its claims of superiority
events.summary: God tells Ezekiel to show Jerusalem her history. She was an unwanted baby left in a field. God said, “Live,” and later married her and dressed her as a queen. She trusted her beauty and gave herself to other gods and nations. She even sacrificed her children. Her sisters Samaria and Sodom did less wrong than she did. Sodom was proud and well fed and did not help the poor. Yet God will remember his covenant and forgive her.
events.detail: Verse 49 defines Sodom’s guilt in social terms. She had pride, plenty of food, and easy comfort. She did not help the poor and needy. Verses 48 and 51 say Jerusalem has done worse. The comparison takes away her sense of being better. Verse 53 goes further and promises to restore Sodom too. The mercy of verses 60–63 is meant to leave her humbled.

events.title: The eagles explain a broken royal oath
events.summary: God gives Ezekiel a riddle about two eagles and a vine. A great eagle takes the top of a cedar and plants a seed. The seed becomes a low vine that grows toward him. Then the vine stretches its roots toward a second eagle. God explains that Babylon’s king took Judah’s king away. He made a treaty with a new king, who swore an oath. That king rebelled and sent to Egypt for horses. God will plant a tender shoot himself, and it will become a great cedar.
events.detail: The first eagle is Babylon, and the second is Egypt. Judah’s king swore loyalty to Babylon and then turned to Egypt. Verse 15 asks whether a man who breaks a covenant can escape. Second Chronicles 36:13 says the oath was sworn by God. In verse 19 God calls it “my oath.” A promise made to a foreign conqueror still bound the king. Verses 22–24 end with a tree that God plants himself.

events.title: Responsibility allows a changed future
events.summary: The people quote a proverb: the fathers ate sour grapes, and the children’s teeth ache. God says they will not use it any more. Every life belongs to him, and the one who sins will die. A righteous man will live. His violent son will die for his own acts. That man’s son, if he does right, will live. A wicked person who turns will live, and his wrongs will not be remembered. God says he takes no pleasure in anyone’s death.
events.detail: The exiles used the proverb to say their fate was fixed by their parents. Verses 5–18 answer with three generations. A good father, a violent son, and a good grandson each stand alone. Verses 21–24 apply the same rule within one life. A person’s past does not lock his future. Verse 23 states what God wants. He would have the wicked turn and live.

events.title: Royal power becomes a funeral song
events.summary: Ezekiel sings a funeral song for the princes of Israel. Their mother was a lioness who raised her cubs. One cub became a young lion and was caught and taken to Egypt. Another prowled among the lions and was caged and taken to Babylon. Their mother was also like a vine with strong branches. It was pulled up in anger and planted in the desert. Fire came out from its own branch. No strong branch is left to be a ruler’s scepter.
events.detail: This is a funeral song sung while the royal house still stands. The lion recalls Jacob’s blessing on Judah in Genesis 49:9. The vine once grew strong branches fit for scepters (verse 11). Verse 14 says fire came from the vine’s own branch. The ruin begins inside the royal family. No branch remains that could rule. The verse says twice that this is a lament.

events.title: The elders hear a history of repeated refusal
events.summary: Elders come to Ezekiel to ask something of the LORD. God refuses to be consulted by them. He tells Ezekiel to recount their fathers’ history. In Egypt, in the desert, and in the land, Israel rebelled. Each time God held back for the sake of his name. The people now think they will be like the nations and serve wood and stone. God says that will never happen. He will rule them, purge the rebels, and bring them to his holy mountain.
events.detail: Verse 32 exposes what the elders have in mind. They want to become like the nations around them. God says it “will not be at all.” He will not let them go. The history in this chapter turns four times on one phrase. God acted “for my name’s sake” (verses 9, 14, 22, 44). Israel’s story continues because of his name, and they do not earn it.

events.title: A foreign ruler's choice becomes part of judgment
events.summary: God says his sword is drawn against Jerusalem, and Ezekiel must groan aloud. The sword is sharpened and polished. Ezekiel marks out two roads for the king of Babylon. One leads to the Ammonite capital and one to Jerusalem. The king stops at the fork and uses arrows, idols, and a liver to decide. The lot falls on Jerusalem. Judah’s prince must take off his crown. It will be given to the one who has the right to it.
events.detail: Verse 21 lists three ways of seeking omens. Deuteronomy 18:10 forbids such practices in Israel. Yet the lot points where God has already said the sword will go. A foreign king’s superstition becomes part of the judgment. Verse 23 says the people of Jerusalem think the omen is false. Their doubt does not protect them. Verse 27 keeps the crown for a future rightful ruler.

events.title: The city's wrongs involve every level of power
events.summary: God calls Jerusalem a city of bloodshed. Its princes use their power to kill. People dishonor parents and wrong the foreigner, the orphan, and the widow. They take bribes and interest and have forgotten God. Israel has become like the waste left when metal is melted. Prophets, priests, and officials all devour the people. The common people also rob the poor and the foreigner. God looked for one person to stand in the gap and found none.
events.detail: Verses 25–29 go through the city by rank. Prophets, priests, and officials are charged first. Verse 29 then names “the people of the land.” Ordinary people also oppress the poor and the foreigner. No class is left out. Wrongs against the weak appear beside wrongs against holy things (verses 7–8). Verse 30 says God searched for one person to repair the wall.

events.title: The sisters represent cities and dangerous alliances
events.summary: God tells a story of two sisters, Samaria and Jerusalem. Both were unfaithful from their youth in Egypt. Samaria desired the Assyrians and was handed over to them. Jerusalem saw this and did worse. She desired the Assyrians and then the Babylonians. God will bring those lovers against her as attackers. She must drink her sister’s cup of ruin. The sisters are charged with idolatry and with sacrificing their children.
events.detail: The sisters stand for two capital cities and their foreign alliances. Each was drawn to a great power’s strength and display. Verse 22 says the admired allies will return as enemies. Verse 37 states the actual charges under the picture. The cities worshiped idols and burned their own children. Verse 39 adds that they entered God’s house that same day. The harsh language is aimed at cities and their politics.

events.title: Public signs join the city's siege with private grief
events.summary: On the day Babylon’s siege begins, God tells Ezekiel to record the date. He gives a parable of a cooking pot that cannot be cleaned. Then God says he will take away the delight of Ezekiel’s eyes. Ezekiel must not mourn or weep. His wife dies that evening, and he does as he was told. The people ask what this means for them. God says he will take his sanctuary, the delight of their eyes. They will be too stunned to mourn, as Ezekiel was.
events.detail: Verse 16 calls Ezekiel’s wife the desire of his eyes. Verse 21 uses the same words for the temple. What she is to him, the sanctuary is to the people. His silence at her death shows what their grief will be like. The loss will be too great for the usual rites (verses 22–23). The text gives the prophet’s own cost one line in verse 18. It moves at once to the people’s question.

events.title: The neighbors face judgment for celebrating another people's loss
events.summary: God speaks against four neighbors of Judah. Ammon gloated when the temple was profaned and Judah went into exile. Ammon clapped, stamped, and rejoiced with contempt. Moab said Judah was like every other nation. Edom took revenge on Judah. The Philistines acted with old hatred. God will hand Ammon and Moab to the peoples of the east. He will lay his hand on Edom and the Philistines.
events.detail: None of these nations is charged with idolatry here. Verse 6 charges Ammon with clapping and stamping for joy. They celebrated another people’s ruin. Each neighbor shows a different attitude. Moab denies that Judah was special (verse 8), and Edom takes revenge (verse 12). The Philistines act from long hatred (verse 15). God judged Judah, and that gave its neighbors no right to rejoice.

events.title: Tyre's expected gain becomes a warning of loss
events.summary: God speaks against the trading city of Tyre. Tyre gloated when Jerusalem fell. It expected to grow rich now that a rival gate was broken. God will bring many nations against it like waves. Nebuchadnezzar will come with horses, chariots, and siege works. Tyre’s wealth and goods will be plundered. Its stones and timber will be thrown into the sea. The rulers of the coast will tremble and sing a lament.
events.detail: Verse 2 gives Tyre’s reaction to Jerusalem’s fall. A trade rival is gone, so Tyre expects more business. The warning reverses that hope point by point. Verse 12 says Tyre’s own riches and goods will be taken. Its fine houses will be torn down. Verses 4 and 14 leave only bare rock for drying nets. The profit it expected from another’s loss becomes its own loss.

events.title: A trading city becomes a richly equipped ship
events.summary: God tells Ezekiel to sing a lament for Tyre. The city is pictured as a beautiful ship. Its planks, mast, oars, and sail come from many lands. Men of many nations row it and guard it. A long list names its trading partners and their goods. The cargo includes metals, horses, ivory, wheat, wine, and slaves. An east wind breaks the ship in the heart of the sea. Sailors and merchants weep at its fall.
events.detail: Verses 5–7 build the ship from the best materials of every coast. Verses 12–25 list its trade, nation by nation. The list shows how many peoples depended on this one city. events.title: Egypt's river cannot belong to Pharaoh alone
events.summary: God speaks against Pharaoh, the great monster lying in the Nile. Pharaoh says the river is his and he made it. God will put hooks in his jaws and leave him in the desert. events.title: Egypt's strength fails across cities and allies
events.summary: God says a day of clouds is near for Egypt. The sword will come, and Egypt’s allies will fall with it. Nebuchadnezzar will destroy the land. God will end the idols of Memphis and judge Egypt’s cities by name. At Tahpanhes the day will grow dark. A second message says God has broken Pharaoh’s arm. It has not been bound up to hold a sword. events.title: A great tree warns Pharaoh about exalted power
events.summary: God asks Pharaoh whom he resembles in his greatness. Assyria was a cedar of Lebanon, taller than every tree. Deep waters fed it, and birds nested in its branches. All great nations lived in its shade. Because it grew proud of its height, God gave it to a ruthless nation. Foreigners cut it down, and its branches fell on the hills. It went down to the grave. events.title: The funeral song places Egypt beside fallen powers
events.summary: Ezekiel sings a lament for Pharaoh. He thought himself a lion, but he is a monster that muddies the rivers. God will catch him in a net and darken the sky over him. events.title: Hearing the warning is different from acting on it
events.summary: God again makes Ezekiel a watchman for Israel. The people say their sins weigh on them and they are wasting away. God says he takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked. A wicked person who turns and makes things right will live. A man escapes from Jerusalem and reports that the city has fallen. Those left in the ruins claim the land, and God rejects their claim. events.title: The shepherd must repair harm and prevent further abuse
events.summary: God speaks against Israel’s shepherds, who feed themselves. They do not strengthen the weak, heal the sick, or search for the lost. The flock is scattered and has become food for wild animals. God says he himself will search for his sheep. He will bring them home and feed them on good pasture. events.title: Seir's claim to the land meets God's continuing presence
events.summary: God tells Ezekiel to speak against Mount Seir, the land of Edom. Edom kept an old hatred and gave Israelites to the sword in their disaster. So bloodshed will pursue Edom. Edom said the two nations and their lands would be its own. Yet the LORD was there. God heard every insult Edom spoke against Israel’s mountains. Edom rejoiced when Israel’s land lay empty. Verse 13 says Edom’s boasting was aimed at God. The next chapter speaks to those same mountains with a promise.

events.title: A restored land requires a changed people
events.summary: God speaks to the mountains of Israel. Enemies have claimed them, and they will soon bear fruit for his people. Israel defiled the land and was scattered among the nations. There the people brought dishonor on God’s name. He will act for the sake of that name and bring them home. He will sprinkle clean water on them. He will give them a new heart and put his Spirit in them. The ruined land will become like the garden of Eden.

events.title: Revived bones and joined sticks answer divided hope
events.summary: The LORD sets Ezekiel in a valley full of dry bones. He asks whether the bones can live, and Ezekiel says only God knows. Ezekiel speaks, and the bones join and are covered with flesh. He speaks again, and breath enters them, and they stand. God says the bones are the whole house of Israel. events.title: A secure people become the target of planned plunder
events.summary: God speaks against Gog, a ruler from the far north. Gog leads a great army with many allies. In later years he will invade a land restored from war. Its people will be living safely in villages without walls. Gog plans to seize plunder from them. Merchants ask whether he has come for silver and gold. events.title: The invader's weapons become fuel instead of power
events.summary: God says Gog will fall on the mountains of Israel. Birds and wild animals will feed on his army. Israel will burn the invaders’ weapons as fuel for seven years. They will bury the dead for seven months to cleanse the land. The nations will learn that Israel went into exile for its own sin. God hid his face from them then. Now he will restore Jacob and have mercy. He will pour out his Spirit and hide his face no more.
